title: Setup Instructions for Students
text:
Follow these steps to set up and publish your research website.


Before you begin, make sure you have the following:

A GitHub account (free at github.com)
GitHub Desktop installed on your computer
R and RStudio







Click the “Use this template” button.
Select Create a new repository.
Use the Owner dropdown menu to select your github user
Name the repository. This will be in your web address! Choose something professional like your name.
Click Create repository from template.
You should now have this newly created repository on your own GitHub.





On your computer: Make sure the GitHub Desktop is open.
On GitHub: In your own repository on GitHub, Click the “<> Code” button.
Select Open with GitHub Desktop.
Choose a local path for the placement of the directory (not a cloud service). For example: (/Users/YourUserame/GitHub/introR2026)
Select Clone.





[!IMPORTANT] 1. Open RStudio 2. Create a new Rproj file in the existing local directory of your repository 3. Open .Rproj file 4. Edit the following files in RStudio




Replace “Your Name” with your name.
Update the About Me section.
Add your research interests.
Replace “your photo.jpg” with the filename of a photo of yourself & by adding the photo to the directory.
Update places that say “link” with the correct internet link or email address, if desired.





Update the descriptions of your projects.
Add links to additional projects as you create them.





Change the title to your project title.
Write your final report.
Replace all placeholder text with your own content.




styles.css * Customize colors, fonts, and other styling options if desired.
_quarto.yml * add new links to the navbar
README.md * This is a place to add information to the GitHub reponsitory, but will not be displayed on your rendered website.
.gitignore * List files here you don’t want synced to GitHub. For example, if you want to keep your data.csv files local and not online list them here
SETUP.md * These are instructions to create this site. No need to modify this file.




In RStudio, you can preview your website before publishing.
Run the following command in the RStudio Terminal:
quarto preview
To render the website before pushing your changes, run:
quarto render



When you are satisfied with your changes:

Open GitHub Desktop.
Review the files you modified.
Enter a commit summary and an optional description.
Click Commit to main.
Click Push origin to upload your changes to GitHub.





Go to your repository on GitHub.
Click Settings.
Select Pages from the left sidebar.
Under Build and deployment:

Source: Select Deploy from a branch.
Branch: Select main.
Folder: Select /docs.

Click Save.





Wait 1–2 minutes for GitHub to deploy your site.
Return to Settings → Pages.
You should see a URL similar to:
https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io/YOUR-REPOSITORY/
Click the link to view your website.





Whenever you want to update your website:

Edit your .qmd files.
Commit and push your changes using GitHub Desktop.
Wait 1–2 minutes for GitHub Pages to rebuild your site.
Refresh your browser to view the updated website.




If your website is not updating:

Go to your GitHub repository.
Click the Actions tab.
Open the most recent workflow run.
Review any error messages if the build failed.







Go to Settings → Pages.
Confirm that:

The branch is set to main.
The folder is set to /docs.

Your website URL should appear on this page after deployment.




Always use forward slashes (/) in links, even when using Windows.
# Correct
[Link](projects/final-report.qmd)

# Incorrect
[Link](projects\final-report.qmd)




To add another page, such as a poster, publication, or additional project:

Create a new .qmd file in the projects/ folder.
Edit projects.qmd and add a link to the new page.
Commit and push your changes.
Wait 1–2 minutes for GitHub Pages to update your website.

GitHub Pages Documentation
Markdown Guide
Git Basics


Need help? Contact your instructor or refer to the resources listed above.

title: How Brain Radiation Affects Blood Vessel Cells: A Single-Cell RNA-Seq Glimpse
section: The Problem: Why Brain Radiation Causes Cognitive Decline
text:
The Problem: Why Brain Radiation Causes Cognitive Decline
Whole brain irradiation (WBI) is a standard treatment for patients with multiple brain metastases. Despite its clinical value, about 50% of long-term survivors develop progressive neurocognitive decline that severely reduces quality of life.

title: How Brain Radiation Affects Blood Vessel Cells: A Single-Cell RNA-Seq Glimpse
section: Hypothesis: WBI-Induced Endothelial Senescence Drives Vascular Fragility
text:
Hypothesis: WBI-Induced Endothelial Senescence Drives Vascular Fragility
Growing preclinical evidence points to radiation-induced cerebrovascular injury as a central driver of this decline. Here, we test the hypothesis that WBI-induced endothelial senescence promotes cerebrovascular fragility, leading to cerebral microhemorrhages (CMHs) that mimic accelerated vascular aging.

title: How Brain Radiation Affects Blood Vessel Cells: A Single-Cell RNA-Seq Glimpse
text:
Why Focus on Endothelial Cells?
Endothelial cells are a key part of the neurovascular unit and are essential for maintaining blood-brain barrier integrity, regulating cerebral blood flow, and preserving normal brain function. Because of these roles, endothelial injury may be one of the main ways that whole brain irradiation leads to long-term cerebrovascular dysfunction and cognitive decline.
This focus is supported by our lab’s previous work showing that WBI induces endothelial dysfunction in the mouse brain and produces an accelerated vascular aging-like phenotype. In addition, senolytic treatment with Navitoclax/ABT263 has been shown to reduce WBI-induced blood-brain barrier disruption, further suggesting that senescent endothelial cells may play an important role in radiation-related brain injury [1-3].

text:
Data Acquisition: From Sequencer to R

Experimental Design

Subjects: Young mice

Treatment: Fractionated Whole-Brain X-ray Irradiation (WBI) at a clinically relevant dose of 5 Gy twice weekly for four weeks, for a total dose of 40 Gy

Timepoint: Two months post-treatment; FACS and scRNA-seq readouts

Method: 10x Genomics Chromium Single Cell 3′ Gene Expression

Figure 1 summarizes the experimental design, including the p16-3MR reporter system, irradiation protocol, cell sorting, and single-cell RNA-sequencing workflow.





Experimental design for evaluating whole-brain irradiation-induced cellular senescence. Young p16-3MR mice underwent fractionated WBI followed by a two-month recovery period, FACS, and single-cell RNA sequencing.

The Analysis: Finding Senescent Endothelial Cells

Focusing on Endothelial Cells

# Subset to endothelial cells

filtered_Lowquality_EC = subset(filtered_Lowquality, grepl("EC", subtype, useBytes = TRUE))

# Remove fenestrated ECs (not relevant for brain vasculature)

filtered_Lowquality_EC_filtered = filtered_Lowquality_EC |> filter(subtype != "Fenestrated EC")

### Senescence Score Distribution

ggplot(filtered_Lowquality_EC_filtered,aes (x = score, y = subtype, fill = subtype))+ 
  geom_boxplot() + 
  #scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 3000), breaks = seq(0, 100, 10)) + 
  theme_classic() + 
  labs(subtitle = "Senescence score distribution across endothelial subtypes",x = "Senescent score", y = "Subtype") +
  coord_flip() + # fill = "Cell Type") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Spectral")







###| fig 2: Senescence score distribution across endothelial subtypes



Key Observation
The Arterial EC and Arterial-capillary EC subtypes appear to have the highest senescence scores, with medians above the other endothelial groups. In contrast, Stressed venous EC and Venous EC show lower overall senescence scores, suggesting subtype-specific differences in endothelial aging

# Apply senescence threshold (based on the calculation)

threshold = 0.5 * 0.168

# Focus on relevant EC subtypes

plot.data.filtered = plot.data |> filter(score > threshold)
plot.data.filtered = plot.data.filtered |> filter(subtype %in% c("Arterial-capillary EC", "Arterial EC", "Capillary-venous EC", "Venous EC"))

## Treatment Effect on Senescence

ggplot(plot.data.filtered,
       aes(x = subtype, y = score, fill = condition)) +
  #stat_boxplot(geom = "errorbar", width = 0.2) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(x = "% of Senescent cells", y = "Subtypes", subtitle = "Effect of WBI on endothelial senescence across subtypes" )







  #coord_flip()
  #scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Spectral")

###| fig 3: Effect of WBI on endothelial senescence across subtypes



Key Observation
The treatment group shows slightly higher senescence percentages than the control group across most endothelial subtypes, especially in arterial-capillary and arterial ECs. Overall, the boxplots suggest a modest increase in endothelial senescence after WBI, with the largest shift seen in the more arterial-like cell populations

title: Siva Sai Chandragiri
text:
I am Siva Sai Chandragiri, a Ph.D. candidate in Pathology at the University of Oklahoma Health Sciences Center and an American Heart Association Predoctoral Fellow. My research focuses on cerebrovascular aging, radiation- and chemotherapy-related brain injury, and the vascular mechanisms that contribute to cognitive decline, stroke, and dementia. Using preclinical models, imaging, and transcriptomic approaches, I study how endothelial dysfunction and senescence impair brain health across aging and disease.



For my PhD dissertation project,
I am investigating how clinically relevant whole-brain X-ray irradiation affects contributes to cerebrovascualr dysfunction in aging and disease. I am particularly interested in cerebral microhemorrhages, endothelial senescence, neurovascular coupling, and treatment-related brain injury.Although whole-brain irradiation is an effective treatment for patients with brain metastases, it can also cause long-term cerebrovascular injury, blood-brain barrier dysfunction, and cognitive decline. Endothelial cells are especially important because they help maintain vascular integrity, regulate cerebral blood flow, and support neurovascular function. However, the specific role of endothelial senescence in radiation-induced vascular fragility remains incompletely understood.
I aim to use single-cell RNA sequencing data and R-based analysis to characterize cell type abundance, identify senescence-associated transcriptional changes, and compare endothelial subtypes between control and irradiated mice. By studying how whole-brain irradiation alters endothelial cell states and promotes senescence-like changes, this project may help reveal mechanisms underlying radiation-induced cerebrovascular dysfunction and identify potential targets for protecting brain health.



My experience includes neuroscience research, cerebrovascular biology, mouse surgery and animal work, molecular and cellular techniques, microscopy, and data analysis in R. I also have experience with scRNA-seq, bioinformatic analysis, scientific writing, poster presentations, teaching, and manuscript preparation.
I am an American Heart Association Predoctoral Fellowship recipient, and I am especially interested in grant writing and research development. After completing my dissertation, I plan to pursue a postdoctoral fellowship to continue building my research in brain aging, cerebrovascular dysfunction, and vascular contributions to cognitive decline.
You can find more details about my ongoing projects, publications, and additional research experience on this website.

title: Projects
text:
*In 2023, I joined the Csiszar and Ungvari Vascular Cognitive Impairment and Dementia research group in the Department of Neurosurgery at the University of Oklahoma Health Sciences Center. My research focused on using whole-brain irradiation as an experimental tool to induce cellular senescence and model features of accelerated brain aging.
Before I joined the project, our laboratory primarily used a cesium-137 gamma irradiator for whole-brain irradiation studies. However, as part of a national effort to reduce the security risks associated with high-activity cesium-137 sources, our institution transitioned to a Precision X-Ray irradiator. This transition created both a challenge and an opportunity: the existing irradiation protocol could not simply be transferred to the new system without careful testing, optimization, and validation.
I completed the required Radiation Safety Training and collaborated with the Radiation Oncology Department to establish a safe and reproducible whole-brain X-ray irradiation protocol. Over approximately 24 months, we evaluated irradiation settings, positioning methods, shielding, dose delivery, safety procedures, and fractionation schedules. Our objective was not only to generate experimental data, but also to develop a clinically relevant protocol that could be reproduced and incorporated into a formal standard operating procedure*.
